theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A client has bought a 220 V, 3 kW instantaneous water heater for a shower. What must you check before agreeing where it goes?
options: The colour of the tiles and grout around it
That a suitable 220 V circuit with an RCD can reach it
Which brand of kettle and toaster the client uses in the kitchen
Whether the shower room has a mirror and a shelf

questions.stem: Why does a 220 V electric range (stove) usually need its own circuit from the board?

The supply voltage is 220 V instead of 110 V at the fan

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: A client in Montego Bay wants a 220 V split air conditioner installed in a bedroom. Explain how you would plan the electrical side of the installation.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first read the unit's manual and rating plate to find the supply voltage, the frequency (it must include 50 Hz), the current and the size of circuit and breaker the maker asks for. I check the board has space and capacity for a new 220 V circuit, and plan its own circuit with the right cable size for the current, the length and the route, and a breaker of the right type. I plan a lockable isolator within sight of the outdoor unit, rated for outdoor use, so a technician can isolate it where they work. I agree with the client and the air-conditioning fitter where the indoor and outdoor units go, the cable route between them, and the route for the condensate pipe, so the water cannot drip onto electrical parts. I plan the earthing of the units, the fixings, and the PPE and access needed for the outdoor unit. Finally I plan the tests: dead tests, then commissioning by an authorised person, and the records.
markingPoints: Checks manual and rating plate: voltage, 50 Hz, current, circuit size
Plans a dedicated 220 V circuit with correctly sized cable and breaker
Plans a lockable outdoor-rated isolator within sight of the outdoor unit
Coordinates positions, routes and condensate with client and fitter
Plans earthing, safe access, tests and records

essays.stem: Describe how you would install a three-phase pump motor with a direct-on-line starter and a local isolator, from delivery to handover.
essays.modelAnswer: On delivery I check the motor and starter against the order and the drawings, and check the rating plate for voltage, 50 Hz, power and full-load current. I mount the starter and the lockable local isolator in the agreed positions, with fixings rated for their weight. The motor is lifted onto its base with proper lifting gear, levelled with shims, and its shaft lined up with the pump shaft as the maker says. I run the supply cable from the board to the isolator and starter, and a flexible connection to the motor, with a separate protective conductor. I terminate the cores in the right order, tighten to torque and label everything. With everything still isolated, locked and proved dead, I carry out continuity, insulation resistance and polarity tests and record them. I set the overload relay to the motor's full-load current. An authorised person then energises it, checks the direction of rotation briefly and the running current, and tests start, stop and the emergency stop. Finally I hand over the records and show the client's staff how to use and isolate it.
markingPoints: Checks equipment and rating plate on delivery
Mounts starter, isolator and motor correctly, with alignment
Wires with flexible final connection and separate protective conductor, terminated and labelled
Dead tests with the circuit isolated; overload set to full-load current
Authorised person energises, checks rotation, current and controls; handover

essays.stem: Compare direct-on-line starting, star-delta starting, a soft starter and a variable speed drive. Say when each would be a good choice.
essays.modelAnswer: Direct-on-line (DOL) starting connects the motor straight to the full supply. It is simple and cheap, but the motor draws a high starting current, often about six times its full-load current, and starts with a jolt. It suits small motors where the supply can take the surge. Star-delta starting connects the windings in star first, which reduces the starting current to about a third, then changes to delta to run. It suits larger motors that start with a light load, such as fans, but the motor must be wound for delta running at the supply voltage. A soft starter uses electronics to raise the voltage gradually, giving a smooth start and lower current, which suits pumps where sudden starts cause water hammer. A variable speed drive changes the frequency and voltage, so it can control the speed all the time, not just at start. It costs more, but saves energy on fans and pumps that do not need full speed, and gives a very smooth start.
markingPoints: DOL: simple, high starting current, suits small motors
Star-delta: reduces starting current, suits larger lightly loaded starts
Soft starter: gradual voltage rise, smooth start, suits pumps
VSD: controls speed by frequency, saves energy, smooth start
Gives a sensible choice for each with a reason

essays.stem: Explain how to install a 220 V instantaneous shower water heater safely.
essays.modelAnswer: I read the maker's instructions first, and check the heater's rating against the supply: 220 V and its current. It needs its own circuit from the board, with a cable sized for its current and the length of run, a breaker of the right rating, and RCD protection, because it is in a wet place. A suitable double-pole isolating switch is fitted where it can be reached but is out of reach of anyone in the shower, unless the maker says otherwise. The heater must be fitted where its IP rating allows, and the cable entry must be sealed as the maker says so water cannot get in. The heater's earth must be connected, and metal pipework bonded as required. All work is done with the circuit isolated, locked off and proved dead. The plumber fills the heater with water before it is ever switched on, because heating with no water burns out the element. After dead tests, an authorised person energises it and checks it works and the RCD trips correctly.
markingPoints: Follows maker's instructions; checks rating against supply
Own circuit, correct cable and breaker, RCD protection
Double-pole isolator positioned safely; IP rating and sealed entries
Earthing and bonding; works with the circuit isolated and proved dead
Filled with water before switching on; dead tests then authorised energising and RCD check

essays.stem: Your team is to install the lighting in a new shop, including LED panels, emergency lights and outdoor floodlights. Explain how you would install and check them.
essays.modelAnswer: I would follow the lighting layout and the specification, and check each fitting's datasheet for its voltage, power, IP rating and fixing method. LED panels are fixed to the ceiling grid or to the structure with their own supports, not hung on the cable. Emergency lights are placed as the layout shows, such as over exits and along escape routes, and are connected to an unswitched supply from the local lighting circuit so they can charge and sense a mains failure. Outdoor floodlights must have a suitable IP rating, sealed cable entries and fixings that will not rust, and are aimed so they do not dazzle drivers or neighbours. All the work is done with the circuits isolated, locked off and proved dead, using platforms or ladders safely. After dead tests, an authorised person energises the circuits, and the team checks each switch, sensor and control works, and that each emergency light works on battery for its rated time. Results are recorded and handed over.
markingPoints: Follows the layout; checks datasheets for voltage, IP and fixing
Fittings supported by their own fixings
Emergency lights positioned on routes and fed from an unswitched supply
Outdoor floodlights: IP rating, sealed entries, rust-proof fixings, aimed correctly
Safe isolation and access; dead tests, authorised energising, function and emergency duration tests recorded

essays.stem: Explain how to install a CCTV system with a recorder, cameras and a UPS so that the electronic equipment is protected and works reliably.
essays.modelAnswer: I would plan the positions of the cameras and recorder with the client and check the maker's data for voltage, power and the cable types needed. The recorder and UPS go in a cool, dry, ventilated place, with the UPS rated above the total load in VA or watts. The supply for the system comes from a suitable circuit, and surge protective devices are fitted on the supply and, where the cables run outside, on the camera lines, because lightning surges are common and can destroy electronics. Camera cables are kept apart from power cables to avoid interference, and outdoor connections are sealed against water. Equipment is earthed as the makers say. I handle the circuit boards and connectors carefully to avoid static damage. Low-voltage equipment is never connected to a 110 V or 220 V supply by mistake, so supplies are checked and labelled. After testing, the system is set up, each camera's picture and recording are checked, and the settings and passwords are handed to the client securely.
markingPoints: Plans positions and checks maker's data
Recorder and UPS in a suitable place; UPS rated above the load
Surge protection on supply and outdoor lines
Segregation, sealed outdoor connections, earthing and static care
Checks pictures and recording; hands over settings securely

essays.stem: Describe how a newly installed machine is commissioned, and explain why the steps are done in that order.
essays.modelAnswer: First the installation is inspected while it is dead: fixings, guards, alignment, cable terminations, labels and earthing. Inspection comes first because many faults can be seen and fixed safely before any testing. Next, with the supply still isolated, locked off and proved dead, the dead tests are done: continuity of the protective conductors, insulation resistance and polarity. These find hidden faults, such as a broken earth or damaged insulation, that could cause a shock or fire when the supply is switched on. The overload and other settings are made from the rating plate and the manual. Only when the dead tests have passed does an authorised person energise the machine. Then the live checks are made: a brief run to check the direction of rotation, the running current against the rating plate, and the start, stop and emergency stop. Finally the results and settings are recorded, the client's staff are shown how to use and isolate the machine, and the documents are handed over.
markingPoints: Visual inspection first while dead, with reason
Dead tests next with the supply isolated and proved dead, with reason
Settings made from rating plate and manual
Authorised person energises only after tests pass; rotation, current and controls checked
Records, training and handover

essays.stem: Explain how to mount and connect a machine that vibrates, such as a compressor or a large pump, so that it runs well and its connections stay safe.
essays.modelAnswer: The machine is set on a firm base or plinth that can take its weight and vibration. It is levelled with shims and fixed with the bolts and anti-vibration mounts the maker specifies, so shaking is not passed into the building. If a motor drives a pump or compressor through a coupling or belts, the shafts are lined up carefully as the maker says, because poor alignment causes vibration and wears bearings. The electrical connection to the machine is made with flexible conduit or flexible cable, so the movement does not crack rigid conduit or loosen terminals, and a separate protective conductor is run, so the earth does not rely on the flexible conduit. Terminals are tightened to torque, and lock washers or self-locking nuts are used on fixings. After a short run-in period, the fixings, alignment and terminals are checked again, with the machine isolated, because things often settle and loosen at first.
markingPoints: Firm base, levelled, fixed with specified anti-vibration mounts
Shafts or belts aligned as the maker says, with reason
Flexible final connection with separate protective conductor
Terminals torqued; locking fixings used
Re-check of fixings, alignment and terminals after run-in, with the machine isolated

essays.stem: Explain the hazards when installing and connecting a heavy machine in a busy workshop, and how your team would control each one.
essays.modelAnswer: Manual handling and lifting are a main hazard: the machine can fall or crush someone. The team plans the lift, uses a hoist, forklift or trolley as the Centre's rules allow, checks the lifting gear, and keeps people away from under the load. Other people in the workshop are a hazard to themselves and to us, so the area is barriered off and signed. Electric shock is a hazard when connecting to the supply, so the circuit is isolated, locked off and tagged by each worker, and proved dead with a tester checked before and after. Stored energy, such as springs, air pressure or capacitors in the machine, is released or blocked as the manual says. Drilling for fixings creates dust and noise, so safety glasses, dust masks and ear protection are worn, and hidden cables and pipes are found with a detector first. Trailing leads and off-cuts cause trips, so the area is kept tidy. The team gives a toolbox talk on these controls before starting.
markingPoints: Lifting hazard controlled with planned lift and proper equipment
Area barriered and signed to protect others
Electric shock controlled by safe isolation with locks and a checked tester
Stored energy released; drilling hazards controlled with PPE and cable detection
Housekeeping and a toolbox talk before starting

essays.stem: As a Level 3 electrician, you lead a team installing 30 ceiling fans and 60 light fittings in a new apartment block in Kingston. Describe how you would plan, supervise and check the work.
essays.modelAnswer: I would check the drawings and specification for the positions, the fittings and the circuits, and check the delivered fans and fittings match and are undamaged, rated for the right voltage. I make sure every fan position has a fan-rated box or support fixed to the structure. I plan the work floor by floor, share it by skill, and pair less experienced members with experienced ones. I set out safe access: platforms or ladders checked and used correctly. Each circuit is isolated, locked off with each worker's own lock, and proved dead before work. I give a short demonstration of the standard I expect, then check the first few installations of each person: the fixing, the earth connection, terminations and the fan balance. After that I spot-check and use a checklist for each apartment. The team does the dead tests and records them, and an authorised person energises and checks each fan and light works. I keep a progress record and report problems early to the manager.
markingPoints: Checks drawings, delivered items and fan-rated supports
Plans and shares work with pairing for training
Safe access and safe isolation with personal locks
Demonstrates the standard, checks first installations, then uses a checklist
Dead tests recorded, authorised energising and function checks, progress reporting

practical1.title: Install a set of fixtures from a layout: LED fittings, emergency lights, a ceiling fan and an extract fan with overrun timer
practical1.brief: As a group, install and connect a set of fixtures in the Centre's training room or bay from the layout and datasheets given by the assessor: two LED fittings on a switched circuit, one maintained and one non-maintained emergency light fed from an unswitched supply, a ceiling fan with its controller on a fan-rated box, and an extract fan with an overrun timer. First, write a short installation plan: the positions measured from the layout, the fixing method for each item, the circuit for each, and the access equipment. The circuit is isolated, every member fits their own lock and tag, and it is proved dead with a tester checked on a proving unit before and after. Share the work so every member installs and connects at least one item, while another member checks it against the datasheet and initials the checklist. Carry out and record continuity, insulation resistance (with electronic items disconnected as the makers say) and polarity tests. The instructor then energises the circuits while the group watches, and the group records the function checks, including the emergency lights working on battery. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Training room or bay with a lockable supply, ceiling grid or fixing board, and a layout from the assessor
Two LED fittings, one maintained and one non-maintained emergency light, a ceiling fan with controller and fan-rated box, an extract fan with overrun timer
Datasheets and makers' instructions for each item
Cable, conduit or trunking, boxes, fixings and switches as the layout shows
Hand tools, drill, cable and pipe detector, torque screwdriver
Lock, tag, multi-lock hasp, voltage tester and proving unit
Continuity and insulation resistance tester, and test record sheets
Stepladders or a work platform, as the Centre's rules allow
photos: The installation plan with positions and fixing methods
The supply isolated with every member's lock, and the tester on the proving unit
The fan-rated box fixed to the structure before the fan is hung
Each item installed, with its connections before the cover goes on
The initialled checklist and the completed test records
The emergency lights lit on battery during the instructor's function test
checklist: Helped write a clear installation plan from the layout
Took part in safe isolation and kept the circuit dead while working
Fixed their item securely with the right fixings, level and in the right position
Connected it correctly to the right supply (switched or unswitched) with earth connected
Checked another member's item against its datasheet and recorded the check
Carried out and recorded dead tests, disconnecting electronic items where the maker says
Used access equipment safely and left the area clean
safety: Every member's lock stays on until all the work is done; prove dead with a tester checked before and after
Only the instructor energises the circuits, after the dead tests pass
Use stepladders or a platform as the Centre's rules say, with a second person footing ladders
Use a cable and pipe detector before drilling; wear safety glasses and a dust mask when drilling overhead

practical2.title: Install a motor with a direct-on-line starter and local isolator, set the overload and complete a commissioning record
practical2.brief: As a group, install a small motor on its base with a direct-on-line starter and a lockable local isolator on the training bay, from the drawing given by the assessor. First, read the motor's rating plate and the starter's datasheet, and plan the layout, cable sizes and the order of work. The bay supply is isolated, every member fits their own lock and tag, and it is proved dead with a tester checked on a proving unit before and after. Share the work so that every member does a part and another member checks it: mounting the starter and isolator; mounting the motor, levelling it with shims and lining it up with its load or coupling; wiring the supply, the control circuit and a flexible connection to the motor with a separate protective conductor; and labelling. Set the overload relay to the full-load current on the rating plate. Carry out and record continuity, insulation resistance and polarity tests. The instructor then energises the motor while the group watches from a safe position, checks the direction of rotation and the start, stop and emergency stop, and measures the running current; the group records these on the commissioning record. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Small motor (single- or three-phase, as the bay supplies) with a base and coupling or load
Direct-on-line starter with overload relay, start, stop and emergency stop buttons
Cable, flexible conduit or flexible cable, glands, fixings and labels
Shims, straight edge, spirit level and spanners
